title: The World of Bees
text:
What Are Bees?

Flying insects closely related to wasps and ants
Over 20,000 known species worldwide
Found on every continent except Antarctica
Play a vital role as pollinators in ecosystems







Note


Bees have existed for over 100 million years!

title: The World of Bees
text:
Life Cycle of a Bee
From egg to worker, a bee transforms completely across four distinct stages. :

Egg — laid one at a time inside a wax cell by the queen
Larva — grows rapidly on food brought by nurse bees
Pupa — undergoes metamorphosis, reshaping into its adult form
Adult — emerges to take up its role in the hive.







Tip


A single queen can lay up to 2,000 eggs a day — outweighing her own body in offspring!

title: The World of Bees
text:
Threats to Bees
Bee populations worldwide are under mounting pressure from several directions at once:

Vanishing habitat — wildflower meadows and nesting sites keep disappearing
Chemical exposure — pesticides, especially neonicotinoids, impair navigation and immunity
Shifting climate — unpredictable seasons throw off flowering and foraging timing
Parasites and disease — Varroa mites spread viruses that can collapse entire colonies

title: The World of Bees
text:
How You Can Help

Plant native, pollinator-friendly flowers
Avoid pesticides in gardens
Support local beekeepers and buy local honey
Leave a patch of “messy” garden for solitary bees

title: The World of Bees
text:
Inside the Hive
Step past the entrance and a beehive reveals itself as a finely tuned piece of architecture, shaped entirely by the bees themselves:

Wax comb — a lattice of hexagonal cells, built cell by cell to hold honey, pollen, and developing young
Brood chamber — the nursery zone, where eggs progress through larva and pupa stages
Honey stores — surplus food sealed under wax caps to carry the colony through scarce seasons
Climate control — worker bees beat their wings in unison to keep temperature and humidity within a narrow band







Note


Even through winter, a hive holds steady at roughly 35°C (95°F) — a feat of collective effort, not machinery.
